paragraphs: It is argued that the best students should be rewarded by their school. Many others hold a reserve opinion saying that rewarding students who show improvements is necessible. I believe that, school should reward both of these students.

Admittedly, rewarding students who have the best academic performance is undeniable. Initially, students have diligently themselves to their studies, they deserve their praises and privileges. This may encourage these students and other to study harder to win the rewards, thereby propeling towards overall academic gains. Moreover, this kind of competition can be seen in almost every aspect of life where only the best individuals are rewarded. Student are used to this reality and thrive in the face of fierce competition, leading them to achieve success in later life.

However, I strongly believe that students who show improvements should be also rewarded. Firstly, only a few smart students can come first and receive the rewards. This may cause others to think that their effort is futile because they can not surpass those outstanding individuals. Therefore, students prone to feeling overwhelmed and disheartened that gradually lose the incentive to study. Secondly, emphasizing improvements can encourage all students to be diligent in their studies and help them to understand that they need to constantly improve themselves irrespective of how well they have been or are performing. Consequently, the constant desire to outdo themselves bring even benefit themselves more than the competitive determination to win against all others.

In conclusion, I am firmly convinced that rewarding students having the best academic results and students who have improvement is necessible. Therefore, it would be unfair to deny the benefits of one in favor of the other.

paragraphs: Opinions are divided over whether schools should reward students with the best academic results or whether it is more important to reward students who show progress. I believe that schools should reward both groups.

Admittedly, rewarding students with outstanding academic results is reasonable. Since students have diligently applied themselves to their studies, they deserve their praises and privileges. This may encourage them and other students to study harder, thereby propelling students towards overall academic gains. Moreover, competition exists in almost every aspect of life. Students can become familiar with this reality and thrive in the face of fierce competition, which may prepare them for success in later life.

However, students who show progress should also be rewarded. If only a few high-achieving students receive rewards, others may think that their effort is futile because they cannot surpass those outstanding individuals. As a result, they may feel overwhelmed and disheartened and gradually lose the incentive to study. Recognizing improvement can encourage all students to work diligently and to keep improving themselves, irrespective of their current performance. The desire to outdo themselves can bring them more lasting benefits than competing against others.
In conclusion, schools should reward both students with outstanding academic results and those who make progress. It would be unfair to deny the benefits of one group in favor of the other.

paragraphs: It is argued that with a rapid growth of technology, ancient artefacts and artworks can be explored throughout computer and public museums and art galleries are unnecessary. In this essay; however, I am a refute this sch of thought.

Admittedly, technology can provide a useful experience with historical objects and artworks. This is predicated, initially, on the assumption that high-resolution images, three-dimensional reconstructions and virtual reality platforms enable viewers to explore masterpieces and ancient artefacts in remarkable detail without leaving home. For example, louvre museum in France offer online collection that help viewer to access to artworks and ancient artefacts easily with lower charge, leading them to have more creative ability and knowledge about art and history. Furthermore, they might believe that some people cannot afford and have mobility issues still access a vast range of cultural and historical heritages.

However, This line of reasoning, I strongly believe that public museums and art galleries are also undeniable. Firstly, online experience cannot replicate the direct sensory engagement of seeing an artefact or artwork in person, due to it can provide, evoke emotions and a sense of authenticity which digital images cannot convey. This can be seen in the way when people see soldier uniform in a war museum, therefore, they can understand about the harsh of war in the past. Secondly, museum and galleries are vital cultural hubs which symbolize the identity of a region. As a result, it is a magnet for tourism and a facilitator of bonding within the community.
In conclusion, I am firmly convinced that although people can access to historical objects and artworks easily by technology, public museum and art galleries are necessary.

paragraphs: It is argued that with a rapid growth of technology, ancient artefacts and artworks can be explored on a computer, and public museums and art galleries will become unnecessary. However, I am of the opposite school of thought.

Admittedly, technology can provide a useful experience with historical objects and artworks. This is predicated, initially, on the assumption that high-resolution images, three-dimensional reconstructions and virtual reality platforms enable viewers to explore masterpieces and ancient artefacts in remarkable detail without leaving home. For example, Louvre museum in France offers an online collection that helps viewers access artworks and ancient artefacts easily at a lower cost, allowing them to learn more about art and history and develop their creativity. Furthermore, people who cannot afford museum visits or have mobility issues can still access a vast range of cultural and historical heritages.

However, I strongly believe that the roles of public museums and art galleries are undeniable. Firstly, online experience cannot replicate the direct sensory engagement of seeing an artefact or artwork in person, since seeing it directly can evoke emotions and a sense of authenticity that digital images cannot convey. This can be seen when people see soldier uniforms in a war museum: they can understand the harshness of war in the past. Secondly, museums and galleries are vital cultural hubs which symbolize the identity of a region. As a result, they can attract tourists and help people bond within the community.
In conclusion, I am firmly convinced that although people can access historical objects and artworks easily through technology, public museums and art galleries are necessary.

Admittedly, one might argue that a state ban should be imposed on sport since even a minor error can cause a death of a participant, such as sky diving. However, this ban may not practical. Moreover, it is unrealistic for a police officer follows every individuals to prevent their dangerous activities. This is mean that a prohibition exists only a paper and it may drive practice underground, causing it harder to ensure basic safety standards.

However, I strongly believe that people should be permitted to do any sport, as long as they understand risks and receive sufficient training. For example, if people join in dangerous sport such deep-ocean diving or bungee jumping, they should register reputable club that have appropriate equipment and qualified supervision. Moreover, children are be shielded by parents from everything which cause children to grow up overdependent on others and it is undesirable trait. Add to this is that make mistake can bring invaluable lesson, standing children in good stead in later stages of life.

paragraphs: It is argued that children can learn through trial and error, while others believe that adults should help them avoid mistakes. Personally, I believe that the freedom to make mistakes should be encouraged, provided that the errors do not involve serious danger.

On the one hand, opponents of the trial-and-error approach often emphasise that adults can prevent many mistakes. Initially, most mistakes are avoidable; for example, children need not get hurt by knives, fire or electricity to learn to be careful. Furthermore, when parents shield children from harm, they can forestall avoidable mistakes and thereby fulfil their duty. By helping children avoid such mistakes in advance, parents can enjoy peace of mind since they have done their best to protect and raise their child.

Those on the other side have their own valid reasoning. Chief of these is that parents cannot be around their children all the time; children need to experience new things, making some mistakes inevitable. Moreover, if children are shielded by parents from everything, they may grow up overdependent on others; this is an undesirable trait. Added to this is the fact that making mistakes can bring invaluable lessons, standing children in good stead later in life.

Overall, it seems to me that children should be allowed to learn from mistakes and prepare for the future, provided that parents intervene and give guidance on important matters to help them avoid errors that may derail their future.

paragraphs: The given bar chart illustrates how much carbon emissions was released from three fossil fuels gas, oil and coal in the UK over a period of 20 years, commencing 1990.

Overall, there was a general increase in the amount of emission sources from gas in the UK, while a opposite was true in the case of oil and coal. Also of note is that Gas consistently had the highest figures from 2000 onwards.

To elaborate, in 1990, around 270 and 310 million tons were emitted from the amount of emission oil and coal in the UK, with a subsequent declines to 260 and 250 million tons, respectively after 10 years. Conversely, the figure for gas grew from 220 to 250 million tons over the same period of time.

Regarding the latter period of the provided timeline, the amount of emission gas continued to go up, yet less noticeably, by a mere 10 million tons between 2005 and 2010, marking the highest period of the entire chart. By contrast, a steady fall was seen in the figures for oil and coal by 30 and 40 million tons at the same time.

paragraphs.text: The bar chart compares carbon emissions from gas, oil and coal in the UK at five points between 1990 and 2010. The figures are given in millions of tons.

Overall, gas emissions rose throughout the period and became the highest of the three from 2000 onwards. Coal emissions declined steadily, while oil emissions fell overall, despite a temporary increase in the middle of the period.

In 1990, coal was the largest source, at approximately 310 million tons, followed by oil at around 270 million tons and gas at about 220 million tons. By 1995, gas had increased to roughly 270 million tons, nearly catching coal at 280 million tons. Oil, meanwhile, had fallen to around 240 million tons. In 2000, gas rose further to approximately 300 million tons and overtook both other fuels. At that point, oil accounted for about 260 million tons and coal for approximately 250 million tons.

During the following decade, gas emissions continued to rise, although growth slowed near the end, reaching about 320 million tons in 2010. By contrast, oil declined from about 260 million tons in 2000 to 210 million tons in 2010, while coal fell from approximately 250 to 190 million tons. In the final five years alone, their emissions dropped by around 30 and 40 million tons, respectively.

task.text:
WRITING TASK 2
You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.
Some people say history is one of the most important school subjects. Other people think that, in today’s world, subjects like science and technology are more important than history. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your knowledge or experience.
Write at least 250 words.

paragraphs: It is argued that one of the most essential academic subjects is history, while others believe that subjects such as science and technology should be given higher priority than history. Personally, whether this view is feasible depends on each country's circumstances.

On the one hand, in countries that are less technologically advanced, the government should allocate more funds to science-related subjects to enhance national productivity. With sufficient financial support, school can be equipped with more laboratories and can conduct regular scientific projects; therefore, this may help more students to develop interest in science. Moreover, students can become competent scientists, researchers and skilled workers in key sectors of the economy; thereby, allowing the nation to progress economically.

On the other hand, in developed countries, science and technology are already strong, focusing too much on science education may be unnecessary. Initially, this countries also face problems such as social inequality, mental health and a loss of cultural identity which are issues science alone cannot solve and history can help students think deeply, understand different cultural and better appreciate their own traditions and customs. All of these areas are important for a balanced society and they can support science its. This can be seen in how Germany continues to teach the history of the World War II to encourage tolerance, critical thinking and respect for human rights among young people. As a result, students become more aware of the consequences of discriminations and conflicts, helping them become responsible citizens who contribute to a balanced society.
In conclusion, both history and science play essential role in education. The priority of each subjects should depend on a country's level of development and its social needs.

Em cần làm mềm kết luận về nước phát triển để không hàm ý rằng khoa học đã đủ mạnh thì không cần tiếp tục đầu tư, và tách câu dài ở thân bài hai để quan hệ giữa các ý rõ hơn.

Lý do về năng suất ở nước ít phát triển và bản sắc, bình đẳng ở nước phát triển được triển khai, kèm ví dụ Đức; một số khẳng định như “đã mạnh thì không cần tập trung khoa học” cần giới hạn hơn.

paragraphs.text: History and science are both valuable school subjects, but the attention given to each may depend partly on a country’s circumstances. In places that urgently need more technical expertise, science education may deserve additional support. Elsewhere, schools may need to give more time to history and other social subjects. I therefore favour a balanced curriculum whose emphasis responds to local needs rather than a single rule for every country.

In countries with fewer technological resources, governments can invest in science lessons to strengthen students’ practical knowledge. With enough funding, schools can provide laboratories and regular projects through which students learn to investigate problems. Such experiences may inspire more young people to become researchers, engineers or skilled technicians. Over time, those workers could help local industries improve productivity and develop new services. For example, a school science project on clean water could lead students to explore filtration methods that later benefit their community. This illustrates why additional technical education can serve both learners and national development.

In more technologically advanced countries, however, schools should ensure that science does not crowd out history. Students also need to understand inequality, social conflict and their cultural heritage. Historical study can help them examine why such problems arose and how past decisions affected different groups. Germany, for instance, teaches young people about the Second World War so that they can discuss intolerance and the consequences of discrimination. These lessons can encourage responsible citizenship and respect for human rights. Historical understanding and scientific knowledge can complement one another: one helps students assess social choices, while the other gives them tools to address practical challenges.

In conclusion, both history and science have an essential place in education. The amount of emphasis each receives should reflect a country’s level of development and its present social needs, while every student should have access to both.
